subject: In-scope systems matrix for SOC 2 audit - hosting delineation

Cc: soc2@acmecorp.com
Date: 2027-06-20T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Request: clarification on hosting scope for SOC 2 evidence

Hi Lauren —

Thanks again for the quick intro call yesterday. As we prepare our evidence packet for Acme's SOC 2 auditor, they asked for a simple, machine-readable mapping that shows which Redwood systems were included in the last penetration test and what hosting modalities were in scope (hosted/managed API, Dedicated (reserved pools), Private/VPC, on-prem package).

Can you confirm whether the November 2026 penetration test covered: 1) the hosted API control plane and runtime, 2) dedicated GPU pools (reserved instances), and 3) Private/VPC deployments (customer-managed infra)? If not all were covered, please indicate remediation status or planned testing windows.

If you can send a one-page matrix plus the redacted PT report (or a redaction-safe summary), that would be ideal. Auditor has asked for attachments or a shared link.

Thanks — appreciate the help.

Emily Wu
Senior Security Program Manager
Blue Horizon Consulting
emily.wu@bluehorizon.com
+1 415-555-0192

Attachment: example_evidence_request_template.xlsx (referenced)

Hi Emily —

Thanks for the clear ask. Looping in Monica (privacy & compliance lead) and Aditya (infrastructure) to give the authoritative scope breakdown and attach the redacted materials.

High level answer: the November 2026 external penetration test covered the hosted control plane and our managed inference runtime (hosted API). Dedicated pools were partially covered — the test team exercised reserved-capacity orchestration but did not run workloads inside customer VPCs or on-prem packages. Private/VPC and on-prem deployments were explicitly out of scope for that engagement.

I will attach a short matrix and the redacted report within the hour. Monica — can you confirm whether this level of detail satisfies the auditor, and if we need to produce a tailored attestation?

Best,

Emily / Lauren —

Attached: "hosting_scope_matrix_20270630.xlsx" (single-sheet matrix) and a redacted copy of the external PT report we can share: "redwood_inference_pt_report_2026-11-redacted.pdf". Also attaching an artifact index (artifact-listing-20270630.txt) that enumerates logs and environments we can produce on request.

Quick summary (from the matrix):
- Hosted API (control plane + managed runtime): IN SCOPE for Nov 2026 PT. Includes public API endpoints, authentication, request routing, inference runtime on managed GPUs, and prefix/KV caching services.
- Dedicated (reserved pools): PARTIAL. The orchestration layer and pool provisioning APIs were tested. Single-tenant customer compute nodes were NOT executed with customer workloads by the test team due to tenant isolation requirements; we ran simulated workloads in a reserved lab pool.
- Private/VPC deployments: OUT OF SCOPE. Private control plane components (customer-managed VPCs) are not included in external testing unless the customer contracts a scoped on-prem pen test with us as part of deployment.
- On-prem package: OUT OF SCOPE. On-prem installations are covered by customer-controlled testing and our guidance docs — we provide an on-site checklist for auditors.

Remediation/status notes:
- Items identified in the Nov report were triaged; most findings were low/medium and remediated by Q1 2027. The matrix includes a remediation column and CVE references for third-party components.
- We can produce a separate attestation letter confirming the remediation status (signed by our CISO) if the auditor requires one.

Emily — please confirm if the redacted report and the matrix meet the auditor's evidence format. If they need a doc-sign attestation or a targeted test of a Dedicated pool running an Acme-like workload, we can scope that engagement and provide an estimated window (typically 4-6 weeks to schedule).

Thanks,
Monica Patel
Compliance Manager, Redwood Inference
monica_patel@redwood.ai

Hi all —

Adding a technical clarifier to Monica's matrix so auditors understand which components map to customer-visible surfaces and where test artifacts live.

What was exercised in Nov 2026 (high level):
- Public API endpoints (https://api.redwood.ai) including auth, rate limiting, and streaming endpoints.
- Managed inference runtime on our shared fleet (includes GPU nodes with continuous batching and KV cache).
- Orchestration APIs that allocate Dedicated pools (provisioning, deprovisioning, autoscaling control plane).

What was NOT tested (and why):
- Customer-managed VPC/private deployments: the runtime image and orchestration docs are the same codebase, but network isolation means external testers cannot reach customer infra without explicit customer-approved test windows.
- On-prem packages: installers and runtime are provided as artifacts; customers run their own tests or request co-ordinated testing with a Redwood engineer onsite.

Artifacts available (see artifact-listing-20270630.txt): log-redaction samples, orchestration API request traces (redacted), and the lab pool snapshot used for the Dedicated simulations. We can map each artifact to the matrix row if the auditor wants a traceability table.

If Acme's auditor needs nondisclosure-protected raw findings, we recommend a short MSA amendment to allow sharing of unredacted sections under an NDA; otherwise the redacted PDF should be sufficient for SOC 2 evidence.

-Aditya
Aditya Rao
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference
aditya_rao@redwood.ai

Emily —

We've uploaded the requested items to the folder (link below) and added the CISO attestation PDF: "redwood_ciso_attestation_20270622.pdf". Monica also added a short paragraph to the matrix about Dedicated pool tenant isolation; excerpt below for convenience.

Excerpt (Dedicated pool controls):
- Dedicated pools are provisioned into logically isolated namespaces with network ACLs and VPC routing enforced by the provisioning service. Hypervisor/container boundaries (KVM + container runtime) are maintained per-node; KV cache namespaces are tenant-scoped and encrypted at rest and in transit. Test workloads ran in an isolated lab pool using the same images and runtime flags as production; the lab pool enforces the same network policies but does not host customer data.
